requirement:
Every Rust function carrying a test attribute, `#[test]` or an attribute whose
path ends in `test` such as `#[tokio::test]`, including those in Cargo
integration-test targets, MUST carry a `{test}` reference to a requirement or
named example under {cite}`requirements.references.roles`, in a comment
attached to it or within its body. A test function without one MUST be a
validation error naming its file, line, and name.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.references.coverage.tests` states only observable validation behavior, so it has no structural obligation that needs implementation evidence. Its clauses are:

- "Every Rust function carrying a test attribute, `#[test]` or an attribute whose path ends in `test` ... including those in Cargo integration-test targets, MUST carry a `{test}` reference ... in a comment attached to it or within its body." This describes which inputs are covered and what they must contain. A validator could find test functions with a syntax-tree query, a regex scan or another method and give the same results. The clause does not prescribe a library, algorithm, signature, type or named interface.
- "A test function without one MUST be a validation error naming its file, line, and name." This is an output convention: the error's content and the condition that triggers it. The text does not say which type or function carries it.

The subject has no implementation edges, and the review roots are empty. I checked the `Implements` edges of the requirement and found none. Nothing here calls for an {impl} marker, because no stated structural obligation is left uncovered. Tests supply the evidence for the behavior. How well they do that belongs to the behavioral criterion, not this one.

The context declaration `requirements.references.roles` defines the `{test}` role. It also sets how references are written (inline or fenced, in comments). It adds no structural obligation to this requirement.

behavioral: Obligations and the tests that cover them:

1. **Which functions are tests.** A function with `#[test]`, or with an attribute whose path ends in `test` such as `#[tokio::test]`, is a test function. `src/rust_coverage.rs#mod[tests]/fn[test_functions_need_a_test_reference]` has positive cases for `#[test]`, `#[tokio::test]` and `#[tokio::test(flavor=...)]`. It has negative cases that must not be flagged: `#[cfg(test)]`, `#[rstest]`, and a `#[test]` that appears only inside a `#[doc = ...]` string. It also covers a test nested in `mod tests`, a test inside an inline module, and a multi-line `fn` signature whose name has a non-ASCII character. I read "path ends in `test`" as the last path segment being `test`, so `rstest` is correctly not a test attribute. It asserts the exact ordered list of flagged names, so both missed and spurious flags fail.

2. **A `{test}` reference in a comment attached to the function or in its body.** The same test covers an attached inline `{test}`, an inline `{test}` inside the body, and a closed fenced `:::{test}`. Each of these is accepted. It also covers the cases that must not count: an unclosed fence, a fence naming an unknown target, a `{cite}`-only function, and an `{impl}`-only function. All of these are flagged.

3. **The target is a requirement or named example.** `a_test_reference_to_an_example_counts_only_when_it_references_a_requirement` shows that a reference to an example tied to a requirement is accepted. It also shows that an example with no requirement is flagged. The subject text says only "requirement or named example". But a named example is defined as a case of requirements, so I read this as consistent with the text and not a contradiction. An unknown target is covered by `unknown_fenced_target`.

4. **Cargo integration-test targets.** `test_reference_errors_ignore_unannotated_helpers` writes a file under `tests/` with an unreferenced `#[test]` and an ordinary helper. It asserts exactly one error and that the helper is not reported. `tests/coverage.rs#fn[unmarked_tests_and_parse_failures_remain_validation_errors]` runs the full `validate_repository` and checks that an unmarked test is reported and its helper is not.

5. **The validation error names file, line and name.** `test_reference_errors_ignore_unannotated_helpers` asserts the error contains the file path, the line of the function and the function name, in the form `path:line: test function name`. The multi-line case asserts the exact (node, line, name) tuple from `untested_tests`, including the non-ASCII name. The whole-repository test asserts the error text `test function bare has no {test}`. `ordinary_functions_types_and_test_helpers_require_no_book_connection` shows that a marked test gives no error and that non-test functions and helpers are not flagged.

I found no obligation without an assertion that enforces it, and no gap.

text: :::{req} coverage.tests
Every Rust function carrying a test attribute, `#[test]` or an attribute whose
path ends in `test` such as `#[tokio::test]`, including those in Cargo
integration-test targets, MUST carry a `{test}` reference to a requirement or
named example under {cite}`requirements.references.roles`, in a comment
attached to it or within its body. A test function without one MUST be a
validation error naming its file, line, and name.
:::{req} roles

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`, and MAY use the `{fixme}` role in fenced form. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. The roles MUST mean:
- `{cite}`: the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition. It is an
edge from the source to the definition.
- `{impl}`: the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision,
performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition
specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining
one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or
producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as
implementing it. A check MUST count only if the definition states it, or the
source could not meet one of the definition's obligations without it; source
that checks it is consistent with a definition, such as recognizing a form the
definition specifies in order to decide whether to run other behavior, relies
on that definition and calls for `{cite}`. A requirement stating a convention
for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by
the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that
collects and reports those outputs.
- `{test}`: the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies:
a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome,
or a named example through the concrete case it describes.
- `{fixme}`: the source acknowledges a known gap in fulfilling the definition. It
MUST use the fenced form, and its body MUST describe the gap. The body MAY
begin with option lines naming issues that track the gap, one per line, in the
form `:github: <owner>/<repo>#<number>`, such as
`:github: rust-lang/rust#123`. `github` MUST be the only recognized option.
A named `{fixme}` MAY appear only in sources outside the book. Validation MUST report
any other option line, a `:github:` value not in that form, an inline
`{fixme}`, a `{fixme}` in a requirement or example declaration, and a
`{fixme}` whose body, without option lines and comment delimiters, is empty.
An unnamed `{fixme}`, a fence of `:::{fixme}` with no name, MAY appear in any
project text, including a requirement or example body, to tie that place to
the issues it names. It MUST have at least one `:github:` option line and MAY
have a description; it is not a reference edge, acknowledges no gap, and needs
no evidence input. Its issues are checked under {cite}`requirements.cli.fixme_issues`.
`{impl}`, `{test}`, and `{fixme}` are edges from the definition to the source.
Code implementations are reviewed as part of the definitions they implement or
test. Citation reviews assess cited source items and book passages under
{cite}`requirements.references.citation_review`.
```text
{impl}`requirements.references.roles`
{cite}`requirements.references.roles`
{test}`requirements.references.roles`
:::{req} rust_item_coverage
Rust functions, methods, structs, enums, and unions need no annotation or recorded
assessment read merely to account for their existence. A missing annotation or
recorded read produces no warning or validation error solely because the item
exists.
`habeas status` and `habeas author` do not report unreferenced-item counts or
warnings, and do not inspect evidence-file Git history to decide whether source
items have been read.
This does not waive the reference-role obligations of
{cite}`requirements.references.procedure`, the annotation requirements for tests
and Cargo examples under {cite}`requirements.references.coverage.tests` and
{cite}`requirements.references.coverage.examples`, or execution-coverage policy
under {cite}`requirements.test-coverage.check.functions` and
{cite}`requirements.test-coverage.check.exceptions`. Actual assessment reads
remain dependencies checked for freshness under
{cite}`requirements.ci.outline_inputs`.
